{"id": "7:172/q29", "question": "How is the Black Stone connected with the covenant?", "turns_on": "Whether its benefit is intrinsic, only obedient imitation, or covenantal testimony by God's leave.", "positions": [{"id": "7:172/q29/p1", "position": "The covenant record was placed in the Stone, which witnesses or will testify for those touching it rightly.", "reasons": "Ali says it can benefit and harm by God's Book; reports give it eyes and a tongue at Judgment. Fatima bint Husayn and Ja'far call touching it fulfillment of the pledge."}, {"id": "7:172/q29/p2", "position": "The Stone itself cannot harm or benefit; Umar kisses it because the Prophet did.", "reasons": "Ali answers Umar with the covenant-witness account."}, {"id": "7:172/q29/p3", "position": "It is God's right hand on earth and a stone from Paradise.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas likens touching it to greeting God; Ata says impurities altered its original state."}]}
{"id": "7:172/q30", "question": "What bearing does the fixed covenant have on coitus interruptus?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:172/q30/p1", "position": "It is permissible or futile as a means of preventing a decreed life: every covenanted person will emerge.", "reasons": "Ali ibn Husayn applied the verse to the practice; reports say a decreed child would be born even if seed fell on a stone."}]}
{"id": "7:172/q31", "question": "What does the covenant teach about human nature and moral knowledge?", "turns_on": "Whether monotheistic awareness is innate and obscured or acquired from later social and psychological forces.", "positions": [{"id": "7:172/q31/p1", "position": "Human beings are born with innate recognition of one Creator, later obscured by parents, society, desire or Satan.", "reasons": "Reports say every newborn is on fitra until parents make the child Jewish, Christian or Zoroastrian; 30:30 is cited. Islahi rejects blank-slate and fear-origin theories, arguing gratitude precedes fear and environmental traditions themselves arise from nature."}, {"id": "7:172/q31/p2", "position": "The newborn is a blank slate and acquires religious cognizance from environment.", "reasons": "Islahi reports this view and argues that tradition itself has a basis in human nature."}, {"id": "7:172/q31/p3", "position": "Human religion began in fear-driven polytheism and developed toward monotheism as knowledge advanced.", "reasons": "Islahi attributes this to modern philosophers and rejects it, arguing that gratitude and provider-awareness are prior."}, {"id": "7:172/q31/p4", "position": "Hunger and sexual desire explain human religion and morality.", "reasons": "Islahi attributes reductions of belief and conduct to Marxist and Freudian views and rejects them."}]}
{"id": "7:172/q32", "question": "How do interpreters reconcile or challenge the literal particle account?", "turns_on": "Physical feasibility, human identity and memory, report authority, and whether the verse speaks of Adam's back or successive human backs.", "positions": [{"id": "7:172/q32/p1", "position": "Literal particles can be rational and addressable through divine power, even in tiny or non-bodily form.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj cites ant speech and mountain praise; Razi suggests indivisible living particles or immaterial rational souls. Defenders distinguish forgetting the scene from retaining knowledge."}, {"id": "7:172/q32/p2", "position": "The account is impossible as a history of fully formed future persons in Adam's physical back.", "reasons": "Mu'tazilites cite lack of space, required bodily structure, accountability regress, Qur'anic creation from fluid and two lives/two deaths; Tabatabai adds soul-body identity, practical reason's dependence on social life, and the uselessness of a duplicated world."}, {"id": "7:172/q32/p3", "position": "The extraction report can be true, yet need not be the verse's own explanation.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Ikhshid says it inspires gratitude and fitra; Ibn Atiyya separates earlier soul creation in reports from later covenant-taking in the verse. Ibn Ashur says reports add predestination, not the explicit wording."}, {"id": "7:172/q32/p4", "position": "The verse and hadith state two compatible extractions, one from Adam and one through later backs.", "reasons": "Razi says neither excludes the other; Ibn Ashur reasons from direct children to their father; Tabatabai says the verse itself already implies both and criticizes Razi's division."}, {"id": "7:172/q32/p5", "position": "The prophetic answer about the primordial event redirects a question about a present rational covenant.", "reasons": "Al-Shirazi proposes this as reconciliation; Alusi calls it good but requires figurative language for eternity because created events cannot be eternal."}]}
{"id": "7:172/q33", "question": "What spiritual or inward meanings are read in the covenant?", "turns_on": "Whether inward response is direct differentiated experience, divine action through effaced selves, or a metaphysical account of fixed forms.", "positions": [{"id": "7:172/q33/p1", "position": "The elect recognized and loved God in a distinct spiritual manner, while other souls met Him through different degrees of veiling.", "reasons": "Al-Kharraz contrasts believers' tranquility with unbelievers' overwhelming encounter; Najmiyya distinguishes forerunners, right and left; Sufi reports make the covenant distinguish spiritual ranks."}, {"id": "7:172/q33/p2", "position": "Their answer occurred through divine power while individual selves were absent, hidden, or annihilated.", "reasons": "Yusuf, Ibn Bannan and Ali ibn Abd al-Rahim say they existed in God's power before ordinary witnessing; al-Husayn says God answered as the hearers vanished; others speak of surrender and effaced self."}, {"id": "7:172/q33/p3", "position": "The taking manifests God's majesty and self-sufficiency and establishes proof without divine need.", "reasons": "Al-Nasrabadi distinguishes earlier from later taking through lineages and calls creation forms moved by divine power; al-Jariri says knowledge bestowed by God enables response."}, {"id": "7:172/q33/p4", "position": "The dialogue is an echo of created existence; God's question leaves room for later partners.", "reasons": "Ibn Arabi says God omitted 'alone' because of natural desire; Alusi objects that reports and leading exegetes affirm exclusive oneness."}, {"id": "7:172/q33/p5", "position": "Pre-eternal intelligible forms or fixed entities answer through primordial capacity rather than later tongues.", "reasons": "Al-Khalakhali distinguishes subsistence from existence; Alusi accepts that distinction. Another scholar describes the exchange as divine manifestation and potential readiness."}]}
{"id": "7:172/q34", "question": "How does this verse connect with its surrounding passage and other covenants?", "turns_on": "Whether the local context primarily widens Sinai's covenant, turns to Arab idolaters, or remains within the surrounding Jewish narratives.", "positions": [{"id": "7:172/q34/p1", "position": "It generalizes the nearby Sinai covenant to all humanity, combining scriptural and rational proof.", "reasons": "Jishumi, Tabarsi and Alusi connect 7:171 and 2:63 with the universal pledge; Alusi calls the wording's shift a thematic digression but prefers a universal audience."}, {"id": "7:172/q34/p2", "position": "It returns from earlier narratives to a universal proof of monotheism and a warning to Arab or Quraysh idolaters.", "reasons": "Razi sees it after Moses' story; Ibn Ashur notes Israelites were not idolaters and connects the ancestral-shirk excuse to the sura's opening. Islahi says earlier nations prepare the final warning and later Israelite example."}, {"id": "7:172/q34/p3", "position": "It concerns Jewish ancestors and their descendants within the surrounding Jewish narratives.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari takes ancestors as Jews who claimed Ezra was God's son; Abu Hayyan lists neighbouring Jewish episodes at 7:163–175. Alusi rejects limiting the verse to them."}, {"id": "7:172/q34/p4", "position": "It links the first covenant with fitra, prophetic warnings and later failures to keep covenant.", "reasons": "Reports cite 30:30, 53:56, 7:102, 5:7 and 3:83; Burhan compares another self-witnessing exchange in al-An'am."}]}
{"id": "7:172/q35", "question": "What spiritual orders and conduct does Sahl connect with humanity's offspring?", "turns_on": "The different spiritual ranks and the effects of their witnessing.", "positions": [{"id": "7:172/q35/p1", "position": "Sahl distinguishes three orders and connects the seeking and chosen to Adam's and Muhammad's lights.", "reasons": "He describes pre-creation light from Muhammad, a million years' worship and witnessing, and the mercy and forward light of those spiritually near; 57:12 is cited."}, {"id": "7:172/q35/p2", "position": "Witnessing faith and divine observation protects the elect from Iblis and shapes their response to trials.", "reasons": "Sahl connects felicity to faith, obedience, asceticism and adab; he prescribes austere food, clothing, mosque dwelling, remembrance, reflection and patience. Missing congregational prayer or pilgrimage is a sign of misery."}, {"id": "7:172/q35/p3", "position": "Muhammad received every station of service granted to humanity and a special form of divine sustenance.", "reasons": "Sahl says the Prophet's feeding and drinking was a divine privilege akin to nourishment, not ordinary food, which he would have shared with family and the Suffa."}]}
{"id": "7:172/q36", "question": "Which further historical details appear in covenant reports?", "turns_on": "Reports add distinct details to the core acknowledgment: decrees, Jesus' pre-birth spirit, mixed groups, and a shadow-world test.", "positions": [{"id": "7:172/q36/p1", "position": "All future persons' names, deeds, lifespans, provisions and afflictions were written or fixed.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi report the fixed decree, with a sealed pen; one report says Eve was f

ormed from Adam's rib during the account."}, {"id": "7:172/q36/p2", "position": "Jesus' spirit was among those covenanted and was later sent to Mary.", "reasons": "Ubay's version adds that he entered Mary's mouth."}, {"id": "7:172/q36/p3", "position": "The primordial groups were mixed after being distinguished.", "reasons": "A report from Abu Umama says both hands were right, both groups affirmed, and God mixed them; its continuation connects eventual deeds with their homes."}, {"id": "7:172/q36/p4", "position": "Some descendants underwent a shadow-world trial of obedience.", "reasons": "Abu Ja'far says Adam's clay was mixed with sweet and bitter water; entry into fire is read by Tabatabai as a metaphor for servitude."}]}
{"id": "7:172/q37", "question": "What is reported about the verse's revelation setting?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:172/q37/p1", "position": "The sura is Meccan, though a view makes the passage through this covenant verse Medinan.", "reasons": "Qatada excepts the town verse; another report extends the Medinan exception through this verse. Ibn Hajar and Suyuti discuss the convention for exceptions."}]}
{"id": "7:172/q38", "question": "What does 'we' in testimony imply about created speakers?", "turns_on": "Whether first-person plural is necessarily majestic or can include a real collective.", "positions": [{"id": "7:172/q38/p1", "position": "A single created speaker should not use the plural for self-exaltation.", "reasons": "Al-Mubarrad and al-Hariri reserve majestic plural for God; a proposed account says God's plural can reflect acts through creatures."}, {"id": "7:172/q38/p2", "position": "A scholar can say 'we' when referring to the school collectively.", "reasons": "Burhan offers this inclusive use, without self-exaltation."}]}
{"id": "7:172/q39", "question": "Can the testimony in this verse ground legal acknowledgment?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:172/q39/p1", "position": "It can be cited as a basis for acknowledgment; actual debt answers depend on wording or custom.", "reasons": "Shurayh invokes a relative's testimony; Suyuti treats the verse as a basis for legal confession. Jurists differ whether balā and naʿam to a creditor's negative question establish a debt."}]}
{"id": "7:172/q40", "question": "What additional general-language or scripture reports occur beside the verse?", "turns_on": "These ancillary excerpts are separate reports or lexical illustrations preserved in the source notes.", "positions": [{"id": "7:172/q40/p1", "position": "Some cited reports concern Quran recitation and its merits.", "reasons": "Baghawi's introduction reports protection from Fire for a Quran-bearer, Ibn Masud's banquet and ten rewards per letter, variant attribution to the Prophet, and Umar's appointment of Ibn Abza for Quran and inheritance knowledge."}, {"id": "7:172/q40/p2", "position": "Other adjacent reports concern a believing maid, omens, soothsayers and prayer speech.", "reasons": "The Prophet judged a maid's answers evidence of faith; Muawiya's other reports discuss divination, inner omens and permissible speech in prayer."}, {"id": "7:172/q40/p3", "position": "A reported set of answers explains days, thunder, lightning, the Milky Way and the moon's mark.", "reasons": "Caesar said only a prophet or his household could know the answers; the moon mark is connected to 17:12."}, {"id": "7:172/q40/p4", "position": "Some lexical illustrations distinguish sit after reclining from sit after standing, near from far demonstratives, and direct from mediated sources.", "reasons": "Khattabi accepts al-Nadr's contextual distinction, contrasts dhāk with dhālik, and says min and an overlap in some usage."}]}
{"id": "7:172/q41", "question": "How are the recipients of the covenant addressed across the passage?", "turns_on": "Whether the address is distributive or historically limited and how closely report wording fits the verse.", "positions": [{"id": "7:172/q41/p1", "position": "The singular address can summon a group by speaking to each individual, while the covenant encompasses all descendants.", "reasons": "Islahi says context can broaden singular address and the divine speaker addresses each person; Qurtubi's general view extends acknowledgment to everyone."}, {"id": "7:172/q41/p2", "position": "The verse's wording can be restricted to descendants drawn from Adam's own loins or to a pre-world universal covenant.", "reasons": "Nahhas reports the former restriction; Alusi reports the latter as foundational obligations against contemporary polytheist excuses."}, {"id": "7:172/q41/p3", "position": "Its interpretation and implications are difficult and the reported wording requires careful reconciliation.", "reasons": "Qurtubi calls it difficult; Ibn Atiyya says longer reports fit the wording poorly, and Abu Hayyan says variants of mode, form, place and time make reconciliation strained."}]}
{"id": "7:172/q42", "question": "What disputed Arabic usage supports the response 'balā'?", "turns_on": "Whether cited poetry is regular enough to broaden the usual response rule.", "positions": [{"id": "7:172/q42/p1", "position": "Balā normally follows negation, and its use after a plain affirmative is anomalous.", "reasons": "Alusi follows al-Radi on the anomalous poem; Ibn Atiyya restricts it to confirmatory negation, while other grammarians simply require negation."}, {"id": "7:172/q42/p2", "position": "Some poetic or contextual examples permit balā after an affirmative, though the evidence is disputed.", "reasons": "Al-Radi records the dispute; Alusi prefers making Jaḥdar's naʿam answer the immediately preceding meeting statement rather than the debated construction."}]}
{"id": "7:172/q43", "question": "What further syntactic details are given for the verse's extraction and answer?", "turns_on": "Grammatical details attach respectively to origin, number and person readings, and response form.", "positions": [{"id": "7:172/q43/p1", "position": "Both 'from' phrases mark origin in successive human loins, before womb development.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur treats both min phrases as origin; Bursevi locates the pledge in paternal loins."}, {"id": "7:172/q43/p2", "position": "Variant plural and person readings preserve the same main sense while adjusting reference.", "reasons": "Baydawi lists Nafi, Abu Amr, Ibn Amir and Yaqub for plural dhurriyyatihim; Baghawi notes the second-person excuse reading follows direct address."}, {"id": "7:172/q43/p3", "position": "Balā's reply is detached in dialogue form after a confirmatory question.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur compares 2:30 and explains the dialogue separation."}]}
{"id": "7:172/q44", "question": "What further features do reports add to the scene and its transmission?", "turns_on": "Variations in report detail, chains, and relation to the explicit verse wording.", "positions": [{"id": "7:172/q44/p1", "position": "Reports give varied modes and forms, but many routes support extracting Adam's descendants.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya cites al-Jurjani's account of touching Adam; Ibn Kathir notes a particle emergence amid water; Ibn Ashur says the many routes have criticized transmitters yet mutually support the inference."}, {"id": "7:172/q44/p2", "position": "Some versions mention written records and witnesses at the covenant.", "reasons": "Qurtubi notes a version outside Tirmidhi with writing and witnesses; Tabatabai distinguishes narrative reports from attempts to explain the wording."}, {"id": "7:172/q44/p3", "position": "A least-punished person in Hell is reminded that God asked only that he avoid shirk in Adam's back.", "reasons": "The report contrasts the easier covenant demand with his wish to ransom himself with all worldly possessions."}, {"id": "7:172/q44/p4", "position": "A Companion feared belonging to the handful assigned to Fire.", "reasons": "Abu Abd Allah wept because his allotment was unknown to him."}, {"id": "7:172/q44/p5", "position": "The common primordial story extends the Adam narrative and has variable timing.", "reasons": "Study Quran connects 7:11 to the pretemporal covenant; some place it immediately after Adam received spirit, and others debate before or after his fall."}]}
{"id": "7:172/q45", "question": "How does Tabatabai test the atom-world account against the verse and reports?", "turns_on": "The identity of the primordial person, time's meaning, memory's role in proof, and authority of apparent wording and reports.", "positions": [{"id": "7:172/q45/p1", "position": "The standard atom-world theory pictures fully conscious future persons in tiny material particles, which cannot be reconciled with personal identity or accountability.", "reasons": "He describes proponents dividing Adam's substance, returning the same persons to loins while knowledge remains, and cites the contradiction of duplicate worldly identity; he says the report-based theory cannot be rescued by ignoring reason."}, {"id": "7:172/q45/p2", "position": "The verse and sound reports point to a real witnessing in a distinct mode of existence, with the scene forgotten but its knowledge retained.", "reasons": "He says the world of divine treasuries is prior without temporal displacement, and uses reports of the Imams to support an actual exchange; essential knowledge survives worldly veiling."}, {"id": "7:172/q45/p3", "position": "A merely worldly metaphor does not explain the past-time framing or the testimony's full force.", "reasons": "He says the addressee may be the Prophet or others, but a setting in the hearers' own worldly life would leave idh unexplained; he rejects reading it only as certainty."}, {"id": "7:172/q45/p4", "position": "Several objections challenge a prior realm's fit with genealogical shirk and the probative force of forgotten reports.", "reasons": "One objection says a collective pre-world existence leaves no polytheist parents to imitate; another says the verse may be figurative and traditions non-probative. Tabatabai answers with initial

ly separated fathers and children and authority of apparent meaning."}]}
{"id": "7:172/q46", "question": "What additional implications are drawn for innate recognition and the covenant's scope?", "turns_on": "How much the covenant itself establishes and whether its unseen scene is literal, inward, or represented through innate recognition.", "positions": [{"id": "7:172/q46/p1", "position": "The testimony depicts human dependence and a shared capacity to recognize God.", "reasons": "Elmalili renders the exchange as self-witness; Wāḥidī calls God's question the testimony. Biqai says a rational covenant can be read alongside an actual realm-of-atoms address if sound."}, {"id": "7:172/q46/p2", "position": "A first covenant alone does not benefit people who reject later prophetic messages.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports the distinction between primordial acknowledgment and subsequent refusal."}, {"id": "7:172/q46/p3", "position": "Some objection to rational insight also applies to literal testimony if divine guidance or continued certainty is withheld.", "reasons": "Alusi challenges al-Turbushti's argument by asking what insight would benefit one without guidance."}, {"id": "7:172/q46/p4", "position": "Sahl says divine knowledge distinguishes future deniers and affirmers and the Hour awaits all covenant souls.", "reasons": "He also says God displayed power to elicit the answer, whose assent concerned creation's purpose and trial."}, {"id": "7:172/q46/p5", "position": "The Day of Alast names the timeless encounter after the opening of God's question.", "reasons": "Study Quran attributes the phrase to Rumi and other Muslim authors."}]}
{"id": "7:172/q47", "question": "By what means was the acknowledgment elicited?", "turns_on": "Whether testimony came through prophets, implanted reason, or direct speech in the earlier realm.", "positions": [{"id": "7:172/q47/p1", "position": "God addressed people through prophets after their reason matured.", "reasons": "Mawardi gives this as an alternative to an immediate primordial address."}, {"id": "7:172/q47/p2", "position": "God gave them reason, enabling them to recognize and testify themselves.", "reasons": "Mawardi lists this alternative; Razi says deniers of the first covenant treat the dialogue as a representation of rational evidence."}, {"id": "7:172/q47/p3", "position": "The direct covenant dialogue occurred as a real exchange.", "reasons": "Razi says those affirming the first covenant read the dialogue literally; Tabatabai notes that a narrator's added wording should not be mistaken for the Imam's own text."}]}
{"id": "7:172/q48", "question": "What is distinctive about the composition of the covenant verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:172/q48/p1", "position": "Its account of divine lordship is especially subtle in meaning and remarkable in composition.", "reasons": "Tabatabai introduces his detailed analysis of taking, distinct descendants and witnessing with this observation."}]}
{"id": "7:194/q01", "question": "Who are those invoked besides God?", "turns_on": "Whether the address fixes its referent to physical idols, to angel worshippers, or to every object of worship; al-Wāḥidī invokes 7:195 and historical worship against the angel reading.", "positions": [{"id": "7:194/q01/p1", "position": "The immediate referents are the idols worshipped by the polytheists.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Ṭabarī, the exegetes reported by al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Ibn ʿĀshūr, and others identify idols. Al-Wāḥidī prefers this because the contemporary polytheists worshipped idols and 7:195 describes beings without functional limbs. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites ʿAbda ibn al-Ṭabīb for the relative phrasing. Iṣlāḥī says statues represented angels, jinn, and stars; al-Bursawī calls them idols named gods."}, {"id": "7:194/q01/p2", "position": "The referents are angels worshipped by a group of Khuzaʿa.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ reports Ibn ʿAbbās identifying angels in al-Wāḥidī; Muqātil specifies Khuzaʿa in al-Baghawī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, and Abū Ḥayyān. Al-Baghawī prefers idols; al-Wāḥidī objects from contemporary worship and the limbs in 7:195."}, {"id": "7:194/q01/p3", "position": "The wording reaches any being or object worshipped apart from God, including saints and images.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī includes humans and other beings; Asad includes living or dead saints, idols, fetishes, and physical or mental images; Kur'an Yolu extends the point to polytheists throughout history. Iṣlāḥī explains that Arab statues represented angels, jinn, and stars."}]}
{"id": "7:194/q02", "question": "What does تَدْعُونَ mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the first use of calling denotes worship, the designation 'gods,' or an actual request; al-Biqāʿī explains why invocation can stand for worship.", "positions": [{"id": "7:194/q02/p1", "position": "It means worshipping those beings.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Zamakhsharī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, and al-Ālūsī give this sense. Al-Biqāʿī says invocation accompanies worship, or that inability to answer invocation proves unfitness for worship. Al-Ālūsī says the object required by this interpretation is omitted."}, {"id": "7:194/q02/p2", "position": "It means naming or calling them gods.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī links this to 7:191; al-Zamakhsharī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, and al-Nasafī give the designation. Al-Ālūsī says the implied object 'gods' is omitted."}, {"id": "7:194/q02/p3", "position": "It is invocation or a request addressed to them.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī lists invoking as a possible sense; al-Biqāʿī ties such calling to worship. Al-Jishumī defines duʿāʾ generally as requesting an act through an imperative, prohibition, or statement such as 'May God forgive him.'"}]}
{"id": "7:194/q03", "question": "What does مِن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "7:194/q03/p1", "position": "It means other than God.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī and al-Qurṭubī state the gloss directly."}]}
{"id": "7:194/q04", "question": "In what sense are they عِبَادٌ أَمْثَالُكُمْ?", "turns_on": "Whether 'servants like you' states literal shared creation and ownership, grants a sarcastic hypothetical equality, invokes human shape, or stresses shared lack of independent power; 7:195 tests how far the likeness extends.", "positions": [{"id": "7:194/q04/p1", "position": "They are created, owned, and governed by God, as their worshippers are.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī calls them their Lord's property; al-Kalbī and al-Ḥasan stress ownership or creation; al-Akhfash, al-Ṭabrisī, and Ibn al-Jawzī stress subjection, with al-Ṭabrisī deriving servitude from subduing and citing 26:22. Qutrub and al-Tabrīzī say 'created.' Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Bursawī, al-Ālūsī, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī, and Shawkānī combine these traits. Ibn ʿĀshūr traces ʿabd from a person owned to every creature, citing 2:178 and 19:93, and prefers metaphorical concord in calling the idols servants. Ibn Jinnī cites 55:6 and 17:44 for created things' glorification; Ibn Kathīr adds that humans hear, see, and act while idols cannot. Abū Ḥayyān insists the next verse's missing organs cannot cancel likeness in creation or ownership."}, {"id": "7:194/q04/p2", "position": "Even if the idols were alive and rational, they would still merely be fellow servants with no right to worship.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī reads a sarcastic concession, followed by 7:195 denying that idols even possess human capacities; al-Rāzī and Abū Ḥayyān report it. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī connect the supposition with carved human figures. Ibn ʿĀshūr reports al-Kashshāf. Abū Ḥayyān rejects only the claim that the following question cancels all likeness, since likeness in being created remains."}, {"id": "7:194/q04/p3", "position": "The comparison rebukes worshippers by setting their admitted weakness beside the idols' still greater helplessness.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says humans surpass idols in life and reason, while a deity could not be like its worshipper. Al-Ālūsī says people admit their own weakness yet attribute power to visibly weaker idols. Elmalılı calls the objects enslaved, senseless structures and says the worshippers themselves resemble them; he cautions against taking human slaves as the intended referent. Al-Qurṭubī and Ibn Kathīr detail the idols' lack of human faculties."}, {"id": "7:194/q04/p4", "position": "They are called servants because makers shaped them like humans.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥaddādī gives the human shape as the reason for the term; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī mention carved human form in their hypothetical interpretation."}, {"id": "7:194/q04/p5", "position": "Every invoked being shares human inability to act independently of God.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī includes human and nonhuman objects; al-Ālūsī follows that reading. Asad includes saints and images. The condition of dependence on divine enabling explains the challenge for al-Qāshānī."}]}
